title: The palm tree
hookLine: alone and in labor, Maryam holds on to a palm trunk, and is told to shake it, eat and drink
carry: shake the tree; eat; be glad

cards: No crowd, no inn, no star. The Qur'an gives us one young woman, far from home. She has gone off to a distant place, alone, and the labor pains begin.
They drive her, the Qur'an says, to the trunk of a palm tree, and she holds on to it, the way a hand grabs for anything solid when pain comes in waves.
And there Maryam, the woman honored above the women of the worlds, says something the Qur'an doesn't hide. She wishes she were dead.

teach.h: WOULD THAT I HAD DIED ERE THIS.
teach.b: Her words, in Pickthall's translation: “Oh, would that I had died ere this and had become a thing of naught, forgotten!” The Qur'an keeps that line.
It lets one of the holiest women in its pages say the worst thing a person in pain can say, and it doesn't correct her. Then a voice calls to her from below.
Commentators differ on who: some say the angel Jibril, some say the newborn child himself. Its first words: grieve not.

teach.h: GRIEVE NOT: A STREAM BENEATH YOU.
teach.b: Your Lord has put a stream beneath you.

teach.h: SHAKE THE TRUNK; THE DATES FALL.
teach.b: Then the part people remember: “And shake the trunk of the palm-tree toward thee, thou wilt cause ripe dates to fall upon thee.” Think about it.
A woman who has just given birth can't shake a palm trunk; it hardly moves even for a strong man. Muslim teachers have drawn a lesson from that. The dates could simply have fallen.
Instead she is asked to put her hand on the tree and do her small part, and Allah does the rest.

teach.h: EAT AND DRINK AND BE CONSOLED.
teach.b: Then three plain instructions: “So eat and drink and be consoled.” Eat. Drink.
Be glad, or cool your eyes, as the Arabic puts it: let your eyes be at rest. Not a sermon. Food, water and comfort for a woman who has just been through labor.
Christians tell Jesus's birth in their own way, in Bethlehem with a manger. The Qur'an's picture is this one: a palm tree, a stream and fresh dates.

how: Muslims read the birth of Isa in Surah Maryam, and dates have their own place in Muslim life: the Prophet ﷺ is reported to have broken his fast with fresh dates.

o: the date palm: the tree Maryam held in labor
a desert shelter made of woven branches
the stream that ran beneath Maryam's feet

games.q: what's inside the scene — tap the pairs.

s: it keeps her words: would that I had died ere this (19:23).
in the Qur'an, Isa is born under a palm tree
the Qur'an's scene has a palm, a stream and dates (19:23–26).
everyone agrees who called to Maryam from below
commentators differ: some say Jibril, some say the newborn child.

games.q: you're Maryam, exhausted, in pain, holding a palm trunk. a voice tells you not to grieve. what does it tell you to do next?
o: shake the trunk and eat the dates.
games.why: shake the trunk of the palm-tree toward thee, thou wilt cause ripe dates to fall upon thee. so eat and drink and be consoled (19:25–26).

practice: If you have one nearby, take a date, or any piece of fruit, and look at it first: the color, the weight in your hand.
Eat it slowly, letting each small bite sit on your tongue until the sweetness arrives, and think of Maryam under the tree, exhausted, being told: eat, drink, be glad.
If you pray, you can say bismillah before the first bite and alhamdulillah after the last.

wordCard.voice: An-nakhlah, the date palm: the trunk Maryam held and shook in labor, until ripe dates fell for her to eat.

orig.note: Arabic: the date palm, the tree of Qur'an 19:23.

carryVoice: Your line: shake the tree; eat; be glad. Tomorrow, Maryam goes home with the baby. Day seventy-two, done.
